Data-Centre Boom Sparks Environmental and Privacy Backlash in Thailand

BANGKOK — The rapid expansion of hyperscale data centres in Thailand and across the wider ASEAN region is colliding with growing environmental and regulatory pressure, according to a new report from a leading sustainability think-tank. The country has approved more than a dozen new large-scale facilities in the past eighteen months, driven by surging demand for cloud computing, AI training workloads, and cross-border data services.

Data centres now account for roughly one percent of global electricity consumption, a share that is widely expected to climb sharply as generative AI scales. Local utilities have warned that several Thai industrial estates are nearing the limits of their grid capacity, raising concerns about reliability for residential users and other industrial tenants. Heat emissions from server halls and cooling towers have measurably increased ambient temperatures in surrounding districts, contributing to the urban heat-island effect that public-health officials are tracking with rising alarm.

Water use has emerged as an equally pressing concern. Several inland facilities draw heavily on local freshwater for evaporative cooling, putting them in competition with agriculture and household supply during dry months. Environmental groups argue that current permitting frameworks underweight long-term water risk and that recent droughts make the trajectory unsustainable. E-waste from rapidly refreshed servers and networking gear is also straining recycling infrastructure that was never designed for industrial-scale electronics.

On the legal front, enforcement of Thailand's Personal Data Protection Act has accelerated noticeably this year. Regulators issued the largest privacy fines in the country's history against two large e-commerce operators for inadequate breach notifications and excessive cross-border data transfers. A revised guideline now requires explicit, granular consent for any AI training that uses Thai personal data, mirroring tightening rules in the European Union and a recent overhaul of India's data-protection framework.

Foreign hyperscalers warn that compliance costs are climbing rapidly and that mismatched rules across the U.S., EU, India, and ASEAN are forcing them to re-architect parts of their global pipelines. Several have postponed planned expansions in Thailand pending clearer regulatory guidance and renewable-energy access agreements. Smaller domestic providers say they lack the legal capacity to keep pace, and industry associations have asked the government to publish harmonised technical standards within the next six months.

Political pressure is also building. Opposition lawmakers have called for a moratorium on new water-intensive facilities until a national environmental impact framework is in place, and several provincial governors are demanding revenue-sharing arrangements before approving new construction. Analysts say the convergence of environmental backlash, tightening privacy enforcement, and geopolitical scrutiny over cross-border data flows could materially slow the build-out of digital infrastructure that the country's roadmap depends on.

Industry executives argue that the long-term direction of travel is clear: cleaner energy sources, more efficient cooling, transparent data governance, and harmonised cross-border rules. The question is whether Thailand can navigate the next two years without losing momentum to regional competitors.
